title: Clam Chowder
subtitle: New England cream and clam soup with bacon and potato
excerpt: New England clam chowder at its finest: clam broth, cream, and chunks of potato with smoky bacon and a generous quantity of clam meat, thickened just enough to coat a spoon. Served with oyster crackers.

recipe.sourceNotes: New England clam chowder is the cream-based chowder of the northeastern United States, specifically associated with Massachusetts and Rhode Island. The chowder using a cream or milk base contrasts with the tomato-based Manhattan clam chowder, a distinction that provokes strong feelings in New England. The dish has Native American antecedents; the early chowders were thickened with hardtack biscuits rather than flour and cream. The potato is an essential component that adds body and starch. Clams are the defining ingredient; tinned clam meat is a practical substitute for fresh clams and produces an excellent result. The key is not to overcook the clams, which toughen quickly, and not to boil the chowder after the cream is added.

content.text: Do not boil the chowder after the cream is added or it will split; keep it at a gentle simmer. Add the clam meat at the very end and heat only until warmed through; prolonged cooking makes clams rubbery. If using tinned clams, reserve the brine and use it as part of the liquid for the best flavour.

content.text: Cook the bacon in a large pot over medium heat until the fat renders and the bacon is lightly crisp. Remove with a slotted spoon. Add the onion and celery to the bacon fat and cook for 5 minutes until soft. Add the garlic and flour. Cook for 2 minutes.
Gradually add the fish stock and the reserved clam brine, stirring. Add the milk, bay leaves, and thyme. Add the potato. Simmer for 15 minutes until the potato is tender.
Add the cream and return the bacon. Stir in the clam meat. Simmer very gently (do not boil) for 3 minutes. Season and serve scattered with chives.
